vignette:
James Chen's Reckoning

James Chen was fifty-two years old when the bomb went off at the civic center in Portland, a building he had entered dozens of times as a journalist covering city council meetings and local politics. He had been standing in the lobby, waiting for a source, when the explosion tore through the east wing. The blast threw him backward against the marble floor. What he remembers most vividly-what plays in his mind with unbearable clarity even now, twenty-one years later-is the taste of copper and ash in his mouth as he lay there, ears ringing, unable to move. He remembers the smell of burnt concrete mixing with something chemical and wrong. Seventeen people died. He survived with a fractured collarbone and lacerations across his left side. He was one of the lucky ones. Everyone told him so.

For the first few months after the bombing, James returned to work. He filed stories, attended press conferences, interviewed survivors. He appeared functional. But around the eighteen-month mark, after his divorce from Margaret had been finalized-she had grown tired of his distance, his irritability, his refusal to go anywhere public-he began to notice that certain things had started to unravel. A photograph of the bombed building, printed in an archive he was researching, sent him into a panic so acute he had to leave the newsroom. When the photograph surfaced, James responded by purchasing the leather chair and repositioning his apartment so his back was always to the wall-a direct attempt to reclaim the sense of control the image had shattered. Each trigger that broke through his defenses seemed to demand a new safety measure, a new way to fortify himself against the next one. The image triggered an immediate spike in his vigilance; he found himself listening for unusual sounds in his apartment for hours afterward, scanning for threats that weren't there. To manage the anxiety that followed, he had impulsively purchased an expensive leather chair that he positioned so his back was always against the wall, allowing him to see the entire room at once. The purchase felt necessary, almost urgent, a way to regain control after the photograph had shattered his sense of safety.

James had come to believe that if he allowed himself to truly think about what happened-to sit with the memory rather than push it away-he would lose his grip entirely. The memory itself felt unreal to him, a film so extreme that his mind sometimes rejected it as something that could have actually occurred. Yet when the memory did break through, it felt like the bombing was happening again in real time: the pressure of the blast, the copper taste flooding his mouth, the helplessness. This conviction that thinking about the event would destroy him made him acutely sensitive to anything that might trigger the memory. When a colleague mentioned an unpredictable schedule change, James felt his threat system ignite; unpredictability itself had become dangerous because it meant he could not prepare, could not anticipate, could not keep the memory at bay. Because he had come to believe that unpredictability would leave him defenseless, the schedule change drove him to spend three thousand dollars on a security system and another two thousand on a vacation he cancelled-compulsive expenditures that felt, in the moment, like the only rational response to an intolerable threat. He responded by spending three thousand dollars on a security system he barely used, then another two thousand on a vacation he cancelled. The spending was compulsive, a way to distract himself from the thought that he was spiraling, that he would never feel normal again.

The more James tried not to think about the event, the more the memory replayed. When he sat in restaurants, he found himself noticing potential weapons-a steak knife, a heavy glass, the proximity of exits-and his body would go rigid, seized by a freezing response that made it impossible to continue eating or speaking. Because the memory had become so intrusive and uncontrollable, ordinary restaurant details-the weight of silverware, the layout of the room, the crowd-had transformed into potential harbingers of danger; his mind could no longer distinguish between the past and present threat. His colleagues had stopped inviting him to lunch. The threat monitoring had become constant: he listened obsessively for sounds that might mean someone was entering his apartment, even though he lived on the fourth floor of a secure building. Years of relying on hypervigilance and avoidance to manage his fear had only deepened his conviction that he was fundamentally fragile-that ordinary people could relax in restaurants or sit with their backs exposed, but he could not, which meant something essential in him had broken. He could not relax, even when he was objectively safe. The hypervigilance fed the conviction that something terrible was coming, that he had lost the capacity to feel genuine emotion, that nothing held meaning anymore. The very fact that he still needed to scan rooms, still needed the chair positioned against the wall, still needed to avoid restaurants, seemed to confirm that he was not recovering-that the strategies he had built his life around were evidence of how trapped he truly was. A specific taste-something acrid and metallic that sometimes appeared in his morning coffee-would catapult him back into the memory, and the memory would confirm his worst fear: that he was trapped in a cycle he could not escape. The very avoidance and safety behaviors he had constructed over two decades-the careful routes he took, the public spaces he no longer entered, the people he kept at a distance-had become a permanent map of the bombing drawn across his daily life, a daily reminder that the event still owned him.

At seventy-three, James has finally come to therapy. His retirement is approaching, and the thought of having nothing but time to sit with his own mind terrifies him. What he fears most is that the memory will consume him entirely, that the feelings he has been outrunning for two decades will finally catch up. What he hopes for, though he barely dares to articulate it, is that he might feel something genuine again-not happiness necessarily, but the possibility that his life could mean something beyond the moment the world exploded.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: Triggers (photograph, colleague's schedule change, taste in coffee) appear throughout, but no paragraph explicitly conveys that triggers directly drive or lead to maladaptive strategies; instead, maladaptive strategies (chair purchase, security system, compulsive spending) are described as responses to anxiety and threat, not directly to triggers themselves.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: Negative appraisals (belief that thinking about the event will destroy him, conviction that he has lost capacity for genuine emotion, fear of being trapped in a cycle) appear, but no paragraph shows these beliefs directly driving maladaptive strategies; the strategies are framed as responses to threat and memory instead.
  e.g. "If she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenceless, staying home wasn't avoidance — it was the only rational thing to do."
  e.g. "The belief that speaking about it would make things worse kept her silent in her sessions, offering fragments instead of the whole picture."
  e.g. "Having decided that her feelings couldn't be trusted, she worked hard to stay numb — and had become quite good at it."
- Memory → Triggers: Memory appears vividly throughout, but no paragraph conveys that the memory itself triggers or activates the triggers (photograph, taste, sounds); rather, external stimuli trigger the memory.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: Maladaptive strategies (chair purchase, security system, compulsive spending, avoidance) are described, but no paragraph shows these strategies producing or reinforcing negative appraisals; the causal direction is not established.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: Maladaptive strategies are described, but no paragraph conveys that these strategies activate or produce triggers; the relationship is absent from the narrative.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
